# Soft Multiplicative Ban Penalty

**Decision.** Charge a banned leg **3× its real length** (`LBBSParams::banned_mult = 3.0`, applied in
`BannedDist`) instead of adding a flat **+1×10⁸ metres**.

**Date.** 2026-07-10 (committed); diagnosed during the P4 modification round in
[[optimization-methods]].

**Rejected alternative.** The flat `+1e8` penalty that shipped first.

## The symptom

The {{operator-bake-off}} ranked all 32 operator combinations for the LBBS solver and produced a
result that looked like a discovery and was actually a bug: `workload_imbalance` came out at **~3.70
for every single combination**. Thirty-two different search behaviours, one number. That is not what a
hard objective looks like; that is what a constant looks like.

## The diagnosis

Per-vehicle workload is summed from leg distances scored *through* `BannedDist`. A flat +1e8 on the
one banned leg made a single vehicle's "distance" ≈1e8 while the other ~14 sat at ~1e5. One outlier
across ~15 vehicles forces the coefficient of variation to ≈3.68 regardless of what the GA does. The
same 1e8 also swamped the objective — every reported LBBS distance read ≈1.01×10⁸, i.e. the penalty,
not the route.

> "the old 1e8 was a single outlier that pinned workload_imbalance at ~3.70 regardless of operators"
> — Optimization Methods/final_project/mdvrp/include/lbbs.hpp, 2026-07-10

## Why multiplicative, and why 3×

A flat penalty is scale-free in the wrong direction: it is enormous relative to every real distance,
so it dominates both the objective and any statistic computed from the scored distances. A
multiplicative penalty stays on the real-distance scale by construction — a banned 800 m leg costs
2,400 m, which is a discouragement rather than a prohibition.

That single change fixed both problems at once, which is why it was preferred to the obvious
alternative of keeping the flat penalty and computing the imbalance statistic from *unpenalised*
distances:

> "Re-tuning the penalty to a proportionate 3× removes the outlier, so **both** the reported fitness
> and the imbalance fall back onto the real-distance scale — a single change serving both goals."
> — Optimization Methods/final_project/output/experiments/lbbs/tuned/mod_note.md, 2026-07-10

The ban *concept* survives intact — the longest edge is still discouraged, just proportionately
instead of catastrophically.

## Result

On the four large instances, best-of-10: fitness moves from ≈1.013×10⁸ to real values around 1.0M, and
imbalance drops from ≈3.70 to **0.200–0.318** — a 90–95% reduction. All 12 instances remain feasible.
Numbers and the trade-off they represent are on [[workload-balance-vs-distance]].

## The constraint that shaped it

The penalty could not simply be handed to the GA. `Dist` has no virtual `operator()` and
`distance.hpp` was held fixed — a deliberate consequence of the performance design in
[[lazy-dijkstra-distance-cache]]:

> "Cannot feed BannedDist into the GA (Dist has no virtual operator() and distance.hpp must not
> change)."
> — Optimization Methods/final_project/mdvrp/include/lbbs.hpp, 2026-07-10

So in the two-phase design, phase 2 explores with real distances and the ban is applied as soft
scoring only in the final decode. The decision is therefore as much about *where* the penalty could be
applied as about its size.

## Why it is on the wiki

This is a **metric artefact caught by an experiment that had no reason to catch it**. The bake-off was
built to rank operators; the flat line across all 32 cells was the evidence that the metric was
broken. Running a factorial design and looking at the *variance* rather than only the winner is what
made it visible — and the repo published the before/after rather than quietly shipping the fixed
numbers, which is [[provenance-and-limits-stated-inline]].
